slides.0.title: Viticulture, sustainability and Sekt Austria
slides.0.subtitle: Sustainability certification and the three-tier sparkling pyramid
slides.1.title: Organic and Sustainable Austria
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Organic
slides.1.highlights.0.content: About 25% of vineyards are certified organic (preliminary, November 2024)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Sustainable Austria
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Launched in 2015; about 11,925 ha (27%) and 655 wineries certified (January 2025 report)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: How it is scored
slides.1.highlights.2.content: About 380 measures across nine categories (quality, social, economic, climate, raw materials, energy, soil, biodiversity, water); each scored −10 to +10, with categories rated red, yellow or green
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Certification bar
slides.1.highlights.3.content: At least seven categories green and no more than two yellow, inspected by an independent body; glyphosate is banned in certified vineyards
slides.1.content: Organic and sustainable are different schemes: organic looks at inputs, Sustainable Austria scores the whole operation.
slides.2.title: The Sekt Austria three-tier pyramid
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Sekt Austria
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Basic tier (called Klassik before 2022): at least nine months on the lees; grapes must come from Austria
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Reserve
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Traditional method with at least 18 months on the lees; grapes and base wines from one federal state
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Grosse Reserve
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Bottle fermentation and at least 36 months on the lees (30 before the 2022 amendment), released no earlier than three years after harvest; from a single winegrowing village (e.g. Poysdorf, Langenlois, Gols, Gamlitz)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Origins of the system
slides.2.highlights.3.content: 2015 was the milestone; it became law in 2016 by ministerial decree, following the Austrian Sekt Committee founded in 2013; amended in February 2022 to the names Sekt Austria / Reserve / Grosse Reserve, with Grosse Reserve extended to 36 months
slides.2.content: Memory aid: 9 → 18 → 36 months; origin narrows from Austria → one state → one village.
slides.3.title: Diploma depth: Sekt rules and the Lenz Moser high trellis
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Reserve and above: hand-picked, whole-bunch pressed
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Reserve and Grosse Reserve may only use hand-picked, whole-bunch-pressed grapes, with juice yields capped at 60% and 50% respectively, and must be bottle-fermented by the traditional method (2022 amended rules)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Brut or drier only
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Reserve and Grosse Reserve may only be Brut Nature, Extra Brut or Brut (≤ 12 g/L residual sugar); Grosse Reserve rosé may not be made by blending red and white. The basic Sekt Austria tier is not restricted to the traditional method
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Lenz Moser high trellis (Hochkultur)
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Developed by Lenz Moser III in Rohrendorf (Kremstal) in the 1920s–30s: rows about 3 m apart and trunks about 1–1.3 m high, cutting labour and cost sharply; it spread after the severe winter frost of 1956 because it resisted cold better. Critics found fruit-zone shading could lower quality, and it is less common today than it was
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Causal chain: training → cost → style
slides.3.highlights.3.content: The high trellis let post-war Austria produce in volume at low cost, matching the sweet, high-yield market of the time; after 1985 the turn to quality led top growers on steep sites to denser, lower trellises for concentration. A classic example of viticultural choices reflecting the market
slides.3.content: Updated Sekt memory aid: 9 → 18 → 36 months; Reserve and above hand-picked and Brut or drier.
What is the minimum lees ageing for Sekt Austria Reserve?
Sekt Austria 9, Reserve 18, Grosse Reserve 36 months (since 2022).
What is the origin rule for Grosse Reserve?
Grosse Reserve comes from a single village (a Ried may also be named).
What is banned in Sustainable Austria–certified vineyards?
Glyphosate is banned on certified vineyards.
